coach_says: You are a bishop down, so a draw is a great result, and your doubled rooks on the g-file give you one: Rxg2+ Qxg2 Rxg2+ Kxg2 Qg6+ and White's king cannot escape your queen checks. After Qe6 White plays g3, closes the g-file and the extra piece wins. When you are losing, look for a sacrifice that strips the king bare and leaves you with perpetual check.

Your e4 pawn is attacked by the knight on f6 and nothing defends it, so Kh1 just gives it away: Nxe4. Worse, after Kh1 you cannot even chase the knight with d3, because Ng3+ forks your king, rook on f1 and bishop on e2. Before a quiet king move, check what is attacked; d3 defends e4 and opens your bishop on c1.

Black's e5 attacks your d4 pawn but also offers a pawn: just take it with dxe5 and you are a pawn up. After Nf3, Black can play e4, kicking your knight and grabbing space for free. When a gambit pawn is offered early, check whether taking it is safe; here it is.
also: pawn push gains time on a knight

coach_says: Black's king is on e7, right on the open e-file behind your knight on e4. Rfe1 puts a rook behind the knight so every knight move becomes a discovered check, and it takes the rook off f1, where Ne3 can hit it. Bd3 instead lets Ne5 attack your bishop and the f3 pawn with tempo. When the enemy king sits on an open file, put a rook on that file.
concept: rook onto the file of their king

coach_says: Bc8 takes your bishop back home, leaves your king stuck in the centre and does nothing about White's strong bishop on d5. Ne5 was the active move: it attacks the queen on f3, so White has to spend a move, and then Bxd5 trades off White's best piece. Look for moves that develop while making a threat, not retreats.

Rxa8 is right. Your rook on h8 was attacked by Black's rook on a8, so taking first is the best way to win back material. You are still worse once Black's queen gets active, but this capture was the best move.
Castling here is as good as d4 or Nc3: it gets your king safe and your rook ready for the e-file against Black's exposed queen. A good, natural move.
Bc8 safely moves your bishop away from the knight on e3, which was about to take it on f5. Bd7 or Be6 were just as good. You are an exchange up and this keeps everything safe.
Kf8 steps out of the check and keeps you well ahead. Re6, blocking with a rook and fighting for the e-file, was slightly more active, but both keep a clearly winning position.

You gave a pawn for a lead in development, so every move should gain time. Nc3 develops a piece and attacks Black's queen on e4, so Black has to move it again and still cannot castle easily. Re1 is not a threat because your own bishop on e2 blocks the file, so Black simply castles and the lead disappears. Against an exposed queen, develop with an attack on it.
concept: develop with tempo on the queen
also: keep their king in the centre

coach_says: Your e6 pawn is attacked by the knight on d4 and nothing defends it, and Rad8 makes it worse: Nxe6 now forks your queen on c5 and both rooks on d8 and f8, and also opens the d-file against your rook. Defend e6 first with Rae8, or with Qb6, which covers e6 along the sixth rank. Before moving a rook, check which squares the enemy knight can jump to.

White's bishops on c4 and d4 aim at your rook on a8 and your g7 pawn. b5 chases the bishop to d5, where it attacks the a8 rook, and after Bxd4 Qxd4 White's queen hits g7 and the rook on h8 too: two threats at once and you lose material. Settle the tension first with Bxd4 or develop with Nf6 before pushing queenside pawns.
concept: double attack on a8 and g7
also: chased bishop lands on a better square

coach_says: White's bishop on h4 has no defender, and your knight on g4 already eyes h2. Qh6 attacks the loose bishop, and if it runs anywhere except g3, Qxh2 is mate. After Bg3, f5 and f4 keep the attack rolling. Be6 is a sensible developing move, but it misses this chance to swing the queen over to the king. When you have a piece near the enemy king, look for a way to bring the queen over to it.
concept: queen swing to attack the king

coach_says: Nxe6 wins material: the knight forks the queen on c5 and both rooks on d8 and f8, and your queen on d1 now faces Black's rook down the d-file. After Rxd1 Nxc5 Rxf1+ Rxf1 you are clearly ahead. Whenever a knight can land with a capture next to the enemy pieces, count every square it attacks.

Taking with the knight looks natural, but after Nxd5 White plays Qxe5, winning your e5 pawn and attacking your bishop on h5, which your knight on f6 used to guard. Recapture with the pawn, cxd5: you keep a strong pawn centre and your pieces stay protected. When choosing how to recapture, check what the moving piece was defending.

Black's kingside pawns are rolling, and g4 is coming to kick your knight from f3, the piece holding d4. After c4, the c-pawn no longer supports d4 either, so after g4 you are pushed into Ne5 and dxe5 and give up your centre. Keep the c3 pawn backing up d4 and use your pieces, for example Bb5 to pressure the knight on c6. Before advancing a pawn, ask what it was defending.
concept: c4 took support away from d4
also: pawn storm kicks the defending knight

coach_says: Your e4 pawn is a passed pawn, and e3 pushes it with a threat to the rook on f2. After Rf3 Qd5, the pawn heads for e2 and ties White up. Qd5 is a good square but lets White blockade with Qd2 and Qe3. When you have a passed pawn and a target to hit, push it while it gains time.
concept: push the passed pawn with tempo

coach_says: With your king on b5 and White's rook on d4, Rxd5+ is check, and after Rxd5 comes c4+, a pawn fork of your king and rook. You end up in a king-and-pawn ending where White's king eats your a-pawn and the outside passed a-pawn wins. In rook endings, before moving your king, check every check White has and whether a pawn can fork after a trade.
concept: pawn fork after a rook trade

coach_says: Your e4 pawn is attacked by the knight on f6 and the rook on e8, and the knight on c3 that defends it can be chased by b4. After Rfe1 b4 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 the rooks come off and your extra pawn is harder to use. f3 defends e4 with a pawn, which cannot be chased away, and frees your pieces. When you are a pawn up, a solid pawn defence often beats a piece defence.
concept: defend with a pawn, not a piece

coach_says: h3 is a fine move: it gives your king some air and takes the g4 square away from Black's bishop and knight. Bxc6 first was slightly more accurate, but the difference is small.
